prompt: The first counting.py put four titles on the shelf and printed counted: 7. Where did the extra three come from?

choices.text: super() ran both the parent's add_all and the child's
choices.why: super() runs the parent's version only; the child's add_all ran once, because main called it once.

choices.text: Shelf.add_all calls self.add, and self is the child
choices.why: Right. Each of the three self-calls landed in CountingShelf.add, which counted the titles a second time.

choices.text: The counter was also incremented by __len__ each time the program asked how many titles there were
choices.why: __len__ only reads the list; nothing in it touches added.

choices.text: Python called __init__ a second time, once for each class in the hierarchy
choices.why: __init__ ran once per object, and it sets the counter to zero rather than adding to it.

prompt: With the second shelf.py (add_all extends the list) and the second counting.py (only add is overridden), a program adds 2 titles one at a time with add, then 5 at once with add_all. What does counted print?
hint: Which of the two calls still passes through the child's add?

prompt: CountingShelf overrides only add and relies on Shelf.add_all looping over self.add. Which change to Shelf leaves its count right?

choices.text: add_all calls a new add_many, which extends the list
choices.why: Then batch titles never pass through add, and the child stops counting them, as in the third run.

choices.text: Renaming the private list _titles to _items
choices.why: Right. The child never touches the list, and the self-call it depends on is unchanged.

choices.text: Making add call self.add_all([title]), so all storing goes through one method
choices.why: add_all loops back into add, which calls add_all again: the child's first add never returns.

prompt: explosion.py ends at 36 subclasses for four axes. A fifth axis arrives: the loan can be ordinary or express, two options. How many subclasses does one-class-per-combination need now?
Why does the class explosion go unnoticed in the early life of a design?

choices.text: Because Python generates the combined classes on its own until there are more than ten
choices.why: Python generates nothing; every class in that design is written by somebody.

choices.text: Because the first axis is always added with composition
choices.why: In the program the first axis is a hierarchy too; the two designs simply cost the same at that size.

choices.text: With two axes of two options, both designs cost four
choices.why: Right. A product and a sum agree at 2 × 2 and 2 + 2; they part at the third axis, twelve against seven.

choices.text: Because a class only becomes expensive once it has more than one method
choices.why: The cost counted here is the number of classes and where a change has to be made, whatever their size.

prompt: The catalogue team wants Book and Film at the top of the loan classes; the fines office wants the fine rule there. How does a composed design settle it?

choices.text: Neither goes on top: item and fine rule each become a field
choices.why: Right. A loan has an item and has a fine rule, and neither axis has to be nested inside the other.

choices.text: The team that owns more classes wins, since its axis multiplies less
choices.why: Which axis is on top does not change the product; composition removes the choice instead of making it.

choices.text: It uses two hierarchies and multiple inheritance to join them
choices.why: That still declares one class per combination, which is the explosion again with more parents.

prompt: CountedShelf counted 4 with both versions of shelf.py. What protects it from the self-call in the first version?

choices.text: It overrides add_all, which stops the parent's version from running
choices.why: Its add_all does run the inner shelf's add_all; what matters is whose add that one then calls.

choices.text: Inside the held shelf, self is that Shelf, so its self.add never reaches the wrapper
choices.why: Right. A held object calls its own methods on itself, never on the object holding it.

choices.text: Python skips method lookup for objects stored in fields
choices.why: Lookup happens as usual; it starts from the inner object's class, which is Shelf.

prompt: A CountedShelf forwards with __getattr__ instead of writing its methods out. Shelf later gains add_many. What happens to titles added through it?

choices.text: They raise AttributeError, since the wrapper never defined add_many
choices.why: __getattr__ exists precisely to answer for attributes the wrapper lacks, so the call goes through.

choices.text: They are counted twice, as in the first counting.py
choices.why: Nothing in the wrapper counts them at all; the inner shelf never calls back into it.

choices.text: They are shelved and never counted, with no error anywhere
choices.why: Right. Automatic forwarding offers every new method without anybody deciding, and that one bypasses the counter.

choices.text: Python refuses to load counted.py until add_many is written out by hand
choices.why: Python checks nothing of the kind; the program runs and the report is quietly wrong.

prompt: An object that holds another and forwards calls to it, adding what it needs on the way, is using ___ .
During the amnesty week every open loan must stop charging. Why is that one loop of assignments in fines.py?

choices.text: Each loan holds its fine rule in a field, and a field can be reassigned
choices.why: Right. Replacing the part changes the behaviour of an object that already exists.

choices.text: Amnesty is a subclass of Loan, so the loans become amnesty loans
choices.why: Amnesty is a fine rule with no parent at all; the loans stay Loan objects.

choices.text: Python can change an object's class, and the program does that for each loan
choices.why: Assigning __class__ is possible and the section advises against it; fines.py assigns a policy instead.

prompt: A student's loan is due on 16 March and holds GraceDays(3, PerDay(75)). It comes back on 23 March. What is the fine, in cents?
hint: Seven days late, before the grace days.

prompt: In test_fines.py the Recording rule answers 999 cents, which no real rule would. What does that number let the test check?

choices.text: That the loan rejects implausible fines from its policy
choices.why: The loan rejects nothing; the test asserts that 999 comes straight back.

choices.text: That the loan returns its policy's answer instead of computing its own
choices.why: Right. A value no real computation produces can only have come from the double.

choices.text: That fines above 900 cents trigger the library's maximum
choices.why: No maximum exists in fines.py; the number was chosen for being impossible, not meaningful.

choices.text: That unittest can compare integers of three digits
choices.why: assertEqual compares any integers; the size of this one is about telling sources apart.

prompt: Which of these are inheritance in the places the lesson says it fits? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: class ReservationExpired(LibraryError)
choices.why: Yes. One axis, and anywhere that catches LibraryError should catch this too.

choices.text: class ReadyNotice(Notice), filling in the abstract body
choices.why: Yes. The parent declared the hole and owns the algorithm around it.

choices.text: class LoanTest(unittest.TestCase)
choices.why: Yes. A framework designed for thousands of children, with documented hooks.

choices.text: class CountingShelf(Shelf), overriding add and add_all
choices.why: Shelf was not written to be extended and never documented its self-calls; that is the fragile base class.

choices.text: class StudentFilmLoan(FilmLoan), overriding fine
choices.why: Two axes vary there, which is why its fine had to be copied from StudentLoan.

prompt: Notice.render calls self.body, and Shelf.add_all called self.add. Why is the first safe for children and the second was not?

choices.text: Because body returns a string and add returns nothing
choices.why: The return type has nothing to do with it; a hidden self-call is fragile whatever it returns.

choices.text: Because an ABC can only ever have one child class
choices.why: Notice has two children in fits.py, and an ABC can have any number.

choices.text: That self-call is the declared and enforced contract
choices.why: Right. A self-call is dangerous when it is an accident of implementation and safe when it is documented.

prompt: Match each language to how a class is kept from being subclassed.

pairs.right: final on the class, refused by the compiler
closed by default unless marked open
typing.final, enforced by a type checker only

prompt: Book and Film in mixins.py inherit the same four mixins, yet one prints a shelf label and the other a barcode. Why?

choices.text: Their parents are listed in a different order, and Python runs the first label in the method resolution order
choices.why: Right. Swapping two names in the parentheses changed what the class does, and nothing warned.

choices.text: Film overrides label itself
choices.why: Film defines only __init__; both labels come from mixins.

choices.text: Python picks the mixin whose label uses fields the object has
choices.why: Python never looks inside a method to choose it; both objects have title, shelf and code anyway.

prompt: Member(JsonMixin) fails with 'Member' object has no attribute 'as_dict'. What does that error show about the mixins?

choices.text: That json.dumps cannot serialise objects with a name field
choices.why: json.dumps was never reached; the call failed one step earlier, looking for as_dict.

choices.text: That a mixin may only be used by a class with an __init__ of its own
choices.why: Member has an __init__; what it lacks is a method another mixin was supposed to bring.

choices.text: JsonMixin relies on a method that only a different parent provides
choices.why: Right. It is the fragile base class between siblings, found only when the method is first called.

choices.text: That Member needed to inherit from Book as well
choices.why: A member is not a book; what it needed was the as_dict ability, from AsDictMixin.

prompt: In Go, a struct embeds two types that both have a Label method, and code calls s.Label(). What happens?

choices.text: The type embedded first wins, as in Python's method resolution order
choices.why: Go has no resolution order for this case; it refuses to guess.

choices.text: The type embedded last wins, as with TypeScript mixin functions
choices.why: That is TypeScript's rule; Go treats the clash as an error.

choices.text: The compiler refuses the call as an ambiguous selector
choices.why: Right. The clash that Python resolved silently in mixins.py cannot compile in Go.

choices.text: The program panics at run time the first time Label is called
choices.why: Go catches it earlier, at compile time, when the call is written.

prompt: Put the steps of turning the loan hierarchy into composition in the order the section takes them.
items: Pin the behaviour with tests that go through open_loan
Name what varies between the subclasses
Give the parent a field for each varying thing
Make open_loan pass parts instead of picking a class
Delete the subclasses nothing constructs any more
trap: Deleting the subclasses before the factory stops naming them breaks every caller at once; they go last.

prompt: Why do the tests in test_loans.py go through open_loan instead of constructing StudentLoan and FilmLoan directly?

choices.text: Because unittest cannot import classes, only functions
choices.why: unittest imports anything Python can; test_fines.py imports the Loan class.

choices.text: So that they never name the classes the refactoring deletes
choices.why: Right. Tests written against the door every caller uses survive a change behind it.

choices.text: Because open_loan is faster than calling a constructor
choices.why: It is slightly slower, if anything; speed was not the reason.

prompt: A teammate wants an AuditedShelf that writes a log line for every title added. Shelf comes from a published package. Which design does this lesson argue for?

choices.text: Subclass Shelf and override only add, since add_all calls it
choices.why: That relies on an undocumented self-call; the second shelf.py removed exactly that and the count went to 1.

choices.text: Hold a Shelf and forward everything with __getattr__, so new methods keep working
choices.why: New methods would keep working and go unlogged, which is the failure the audit exists to prevent.

choices.text: Hold a Shelf and write out each method it offers, logging in each one
choices.why: Right. It depends only on what Shelf's methods do, and a new method is something the wrapper decides to offer.

choices.text: Copy Shelf's source into the project and add the logging to it
choices.why: That forks the package: every fix upstream has to be copied by hand from then on.

prompt: The library starts lending e-readers for 21 days, with the student grace days as usual. In the composed loans.py, what has to change?

choices.text: open_loan learns one more loan length, and nothing else changes
choices.why: Right. Length and fine rule are separate parts, so the new item reuses GraceDays unchanged.

choices.text: Two new classes, EReaderLoan and StudentEReaderLoan
choices.why: That is what the old hierarchy would have needed; the composed one has no class per kind of loan.

choices.text: A subclass of GraceDays that knows about e-readers
choices.why: The grace rule does not care what was lent; it only sees days late.

choices.text: A rewrite of test_loans.py, because every one of its tests names a loan class
choices.why: None of them names a class; they all go through open_loan, which is why they survived the refactoring.

prompt: A correct change inside a parent breaks a subclass that relied on the parent calling its own methods. This is called the fragile ___ class problem.
